title: Sabotage
text: “Bubu!”

So, whether Keel was angry about not being allowed on the ship or not, I couldn’t quite tell, but she’d resumed playing with Big Sister and the village children. Playing so innocently. It was around this point—roughly a month from now—that she’d start being put to proper work.

Hmm… I’d always just sort of taken it for granted, but it seemed she really could be treated as quite the diligent worker. Especially regarding Keel—Father had praised her as valuable enough in sales to rival Filo-tan herself, which stung a little, I must admit. I’d been rooting for Filo-tan too, but it was hard to prop her up with just me and the Filo-tan Fan Club members alone. Last loop, Keel had felt rather more childlike.

But in that timeline, Keel had been a dog who’d gone on a cooking journey with Ren, so her current form differed quite a bit. What I could recall was something like a shop mascot dog, working the counter alongside someone called Luft. I remembered Luft sneaking bites of food and Ren yipping in protest. “We’re not a sideshow!” Ren the inult had protested—that scene came back to me now. That was a few months into the future.
I’d rather such a future never come to pass—not under the current circumstances, anyway. Better to let Big Sister and the others live peacefully, same as last loop.
“…Yes, I suppose so.”

In my memory, Big Sister seemed to agree, though with a touch of worry in her voice. Hmm… I wondered how the Big Sister from the very first world would judge the decision I was making now. If my meddling ever came to light, it’d be wise to have laid the groundwork for forgiveness beforehand. At the very least, the village should remain peaceful, and Big Sister and Father ought to stay together—kidnapping was absolutely out of the question.
“Indeed, that’s not something you’d do. If anything, it looks almost unnaturally deliberate, the way you keep Naofumi-sama and me apart.”

That felt like something Big Sister had grumbled about, back when I told her of my adventures in the first world. In the previous loop, there hadn’t been anyone resembling actual parents living peacefully in the village at this point in time—but Older Sister had filled that role, living peacefully as a stand-in parent. Father and the others had been nearby, helping with reconstruction, but Big Sister’s growth afterward had been gradual.

Still, amid helping with the circus’s reconstruction efforts and serving Father and the others, she’d once tried to make herself a bunny-girl-style outfit to wait tables in, only to be stopped. She’d worn a sulky face after being told, gently but firmly, that it was dangerous in all sorts of ways. Big Sister and the others had been full of mischief back then, troubling Father and company with one scheme after another. In any case, to protect their peace this loop, I had to ensure the ships couldn’t set sail—by destroying them.

And so, as the sun set and preparations for tomorrow’s departure were complete, the sailors finished their meals at home and settled into lively chatter at the tavern. From a distance, I caught a glimpse of Older Sister heading toward the tavern as well.

…Now was the time. Several ships lined the harbor—a sign of just how large-scale this fishing operation was. It pained my heart, but I slipped into the sea and drove my spear through the hulls one by one, punching great holes clean through. Doh-gon! Doh-gon! I made quick work of destroying every ship in the village, and then, just to be safe, I skewered the smaller rowboats too with an Aiming Lancer. Clang clang clang! The alarm bells rang out across the village.
“Th-this is bad! The ships are sinking one after another! Someone’s put holes in the hulls!”
“What’s going on!?”
“Is it an attack!? Everyone, grab your weapons and stand ready!”
Hearing the commotion, the villagers armed themselves and went searching, bloodshot-eyed, for the one who’d sunk their ships—namely, me.
“Sadeena.”
“I know, I know!”

Splash—Older Sister dove into the sea. But by then I’d already finished sinking every ship in the village. All that remained was the fleet in Éclair’s town. Truly, it pained me. I’d make what amends I could later—funnel the money I’d earned into “donations” for both the village and the town.

As for the town, I tried my best to avoid harming anyone while skewering every docked ship with Aiming Lancer. Screams rang out alongside the roar of burning ships and cries of terror. …I could hardly call this the right thing to do, but considering the danger of the waves, I couldn’t afford to let the sailors or anyone else head out to sea. At the very least, this should keep them grounded for several days.

The next day, if there were still ships in the harbor, I’d have to break through whatever watch network was in place and sink them too. It was agonizing, but it was the only thing I could do right now. After all, I didn’t think it wise to reveal myself as a Hero just yet. Even if I claimed to be a Hero from the future and tried to stop the voyage outright, the flow of events probably wouldn’t allow it anyway. And so, once every last ship had been sunk, the noble who appeared to be Éclair’s parent, along with an elderly lizardman standing beside him, came down to the harbor to check on the grieving townsfolk whose ships had gone down.
“Just who in the world would do such a thing…”
He surveyed the surroundings with a grave expression as fishermen and merchants lamented their losses.
“Casualties?”
“Some were injured during the evacuation, but thankfully, no deaths.”
Hearing that, he furrowed his brow.
“Did anyone see who sank the ships?”
“No one knows. Some say light rained down from nowhere—no, from the sky, like shooting stars—and pierced the ships. That’s the only testimony we have.”
“Magic, then… Whatever the case, to strike with this much force, so suddenly…”
“Seaetto-sama! It has to be those Melromarc bastards! Trying to sabotage our work like this—”
“But… even so, hm.”
“The neighboring village has reported similar damage! And by the timing, it seems they were hit even earlier.”

Reports of the damage kept pouring in. Oh? It seemed Crocodile Guy was the one delivering this report. Though, perhaps out of guilt, he kept his hood pulled low, trying his best to hide his face and body.
“For now, maintain the alert status!”

Amid the flames and the efforts to extinguish the sinking ships, the noble who appeared to be Éclair’s parent issued swift orders. Hmm. So that must be Crocodile Guy’s father. Fairly solid build, but quite aged. Old enough, in fact, that compared to Crocodile Guy, he looked more like a grandfather than a father.

And so the commotion over the sunken ships in Éclair’s family’s territory spread far and wide. People gathered as if for an emergency council, and discussion soon dissolved into argument. My conscience ached. Truly, it pained me.

Meanwhile, the man who appeared to be Big Sister’s father was giving his report to the noble who seemed to be Éclair’s parent. Ugh… Even Older Sister was there. Given the danger, I layered Cloaking Lance and Fire Mirage over myself with great care. I couldn’t afford to be found out. Older Sister kept glancing around, her eyes darting here and there.
Even at empty patches of nothing. Did she sense something there?
“This has become quite the troublesome situation.”
“It’s a blessing there were no deaths, but… what are we to do about this?”
The council carried on in that vein.
“The ships docked in your village—were they pierced by light as well?”
“No, while the crew was out drinking at the tavern, a great hole simply opened in the hull and it sank. That’s the testimony of the one left behind to watch the ship.”
“Hmm… just what could the culprits possibly be after…”
“The village folk are in for a sleepless night, I imagine.”

It was true—there were those grieving over the sunken ships. Even Big Sister’s friends mourned as if it had happened to them. Even knowing it was to prevent casualties, I couldn’t help but feel a pang of regret over whether this had truly been the right choice.
“Given the circumstances… venturing out for deep-sea fishing will be difficult.”

There it was. That was exactly the point. Those who’d gone out to fish apparently hadn’t come back—so, considering the danger of the waves, I wanted them to stay in the village. And for that, I’d steeled my heart and done what needed to be done.
